title: Fifteen Golds in Mersin: India's Young Para-Shuttlers Just Announced the Next Generation
excerpt: India finished the 2026 World Abilitysport Youth Games in Türkiye with 27 para-badminton medals — 15 of them gold — spread across every classification, a haul that points to a pipeline far deeper than its Paralympic stars alone.
body:
India's para-badminton story has, for years, belonged to a handful of household names — Pramod Bhagat, Krishna Nagar, Sukant Kadam, Manisha Ramadass. This week in Mersin, on Türkiye's Mediterranean coast, a far younger group served notice that the next chapter is already being written. India closed the 2026 World Abilitysport Youth Games with 27 para-badminton medals: 15 gold, nine silver and three bronze, a return that ranked among the most dominant of any nation at the event.

What made the haul striking was not just its size but its spread. The medals came across the full sweep of para-badminton classifications — the wheelchair categories WH1 and WH2, the standing lower-limb classes SL3 and SL4, the upper-limb class SU5, and the short-stature category SH6. A country can win medals by being deep in one event. India won them everywhere, a sign of a system producing talent across the disability spectrum rather than around a single star.


![Pramod Bhagat — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/51/Pramod_Bhagat.jpg)


## The Teenagers Who Led the Charge

Haris Mythili Srikumar was the standout, walking away with three gold medals. He took the men's singles WH2 title, then partnered Nitin Yadav to win the men's doubles WH1–WH2, before completing his set in the mixed doubles WH1–WH2. For a youth athlete to dominate a wheelchair category across singles and both doubles disciplines is the kind of week that marks a player as one to track all the way to senior international level.



> **"He took the men's singles WH2 title, then partnered Nitin Yadav to win the men's doubles WH1–WH2, before completing his set in the mixed doubles WH1–WH2."**



![Sukant Kadam — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/a6/Sukant_Kadam_IND_AS7_6216.jpg)


Akash Ranjan Mund was not far behind, claiming the men's singles SL3 gold and adding the mixed doubles SL3–SU5 title alongside Koshika Devda. Aryan Sharma won the men's singles SL4 crown and a second gold in the men's doubles SL3–SU5 with Bibhasindhu, while Shivangi Pandey topped the women's singles SL4 podium. Tulika Jadhav took the women's singles SL3 gold, and Gopesh Jhalani won the men's singles SU5.

The short-stature SH6 category proved especially fruitful. Prem Chand Potnuru won the men's singles and then teamed with Harshit Rajput for the men's doubles title. Manisha Patel matched the multi-gold haul of her teammates, winning the women's singles SH6 and the mixed doubles SH6 alongside Prem. Samaira Kanwat rounded out the gold rush with victory in the women's doubles SL3–SU5.


![Manisha Ramadass — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/97/Manisha_Ramadass_in_September_2024.jpg)


## Depth Behind the Gold

The silver and bronze medals told their own story of strength in numbers. Nitin Yadav added silvers in the men's singles and mixed doubles WH2; Bibhasindhu and Samaira Kanwat reached singles finals in SL3; Koshika Devda finished runner-up in the women's singles SU5; and several doubles pairings pushed deep into their draws. The three bronzes — Bibhasindhu and Nazliin and the pairing of Tulika Jadhav and Gopesh Jhalani in mixed doubles SL3–SU5, plus Harshit Rajput in the men's singles SH6 — underlined just how many of India's young players were genuine podium contenders rather than passengers.

That breadth matters more than any single title. India's senior para-badminton program already ranks among the best in the world, but its long-term health depends on a steady supply of young athletes ready to graduate into it. A 27-medal week at a global youth event, spread across classifications, is exactly the evidence selectors and federations look for.

## Why the Diaspora Should Care

For Indians abroad, the rise of para-sport carries a meaning that goes beyond the medal table. Many NRI families are raising children in Western school systems built around inclusion and accessibility, where para-sport is visible and celebrated. Watching India — a country still building that infrastructure — produce world-class young para-athletes is both a point of pride and a sign that the pathway now exists back home, not only in Europe or North America.

It is also a reminder that India's sporting identity is broadening. The diaspora's attention is fixed, understandably, on cricket and increasingly on football's World Cup summer. But the athletes who often deliver India's most emotional global moments — the para-shuttlers, para-athletes and Paralympians — are quietly building a base that will define the country's medal hopes for the decade ahead. In Mersin this week, that base just got a great deal deeper.
